parts.label: Understand
parts.title: Separate demonstrated work from case study
parts.body:
A career evidence package has two kinds of material. The capstone shows how you reason through an enterprise problem. Work you actually did shows how you acted with real authority, constraints, colleagues, and outcomes. Label the capstone hypothetical or independently researched on every artifact where a reader might mistake it for a shipped program. Do not claim a forecast as realized savings or present a simulated board meeting as a real board decision.

Choose artifacts that let an interviewer examine judgment: a two-page strategy memo, board decision deck, architecture one-pager, governance record, and value scorecard. Each should carry scope, assumptions, decision owner, tradeoff, evidence, and next gate. Remove confidential employer or customer information from any real work and respect permission to share it. A short redacted summary may be safer and clearer than a former employer's slide.

Write a two-sentence caption for each artifact: what decision it supported and which part you personally owned. Interviewers need to distinguish your contribution from a team's result. A CAIO candidate can explain how they coordinated peers without pretending to have held another executive's authority.

example.title: An honest caption
example.body: Hypothetical capstone, Canadian insurer: I designed a staged investment recommendation and the evaluation gates for an internal claims assistant. The budget and outcomes are illustrative; no insurer deployed this plan. In actual work, I led a comparable decision review for a different internal workflow, described separately.

exercise.title: Audit five artifacts
exercise.body: For each artifact, write status (real, redacted, or hypothetical), your role, decision, evidence, and outcome or forecast. Ask a peer to flag any sentence that could imply the capstone was deployed.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: documented roles and evidence

parts.label: Practice
parts.title: Write leadership stories with decisions in them
parts.body:
Prepare six stories from real experience where possible: strategy, investment, peer conflict, technical judgment, risk response, and organizational change. A useful story names the situation and stakes, the decision you owned, alternatives you considered, evidence available at the time, who disagreed, your action, observed result, and what you would change. If you lack a direct AI example, use an adjacent transformation or risk decision and explain the limits of the analogy.

Keep cause and contribution precise. 'We improved adoption' hides your action and can overclaim causation. Say which intervention you led, how adoption was measured, what else changed, and what happened after. A failed experiment can show strong judgment if you recognized the signal, stopped spending, protected users, and learned something reusable.

Make a two-minute version and a deeper follow-up for each story. Do not memorize theatrical phrasing. Have numbers and decisions ready. An interviewer may ask what the CFO, security lead, or frontline manager would say about your account; the story should withstand that perspective.

example.title: A fictional practice story
example.body: Fictional rehearsal only: a product lead wanted a wider assistant launch while a security lead disputed vendor retention terms. The candidate proposes a limited test with approved non-customer data, a contract review, and a later launch gate. This story is an interview drill, not evidence that the candidate led a real program. Replace it with a truthful example from your own work before using it as a behavioral interview answer.

exercise.title: Draft two contrasting stories
exercise.body: Write one successful decision and one stopped or narrowed initiative. For each, name your authority, dissenting view, evidence, outcome, and lesson. Have a peer ask what you would do if the same evidence appeared again.

sources: Harvard Mignone Center: interviewing and behavioral stories
OECD AI Principles: roles and accountability

parts.label: Operate
parts.title: Tailor the package to the seat
parts.body:
A CAIO interview can come from a CEO, board member, CFO, CIO, or risk leader. The same evidence should answer different questions without changing facts. A CEO may want the strategic thesis and how the portfolio changes performance. A CFO will trace assumptions to funding gates. A CIO will probe architecture and support. A CISO and privacy lead will ask who has authority when a control fails. Board members will look for concise oversight choices and candor about material uncertainty.

Build a small evidence index mapping each claim to an artifact and page. If you say you can govern multinational AI, point to the case's EU and Canadian use maps and explain that counsel must verify current law for an actual deployment. If you say you can realize value, show the baseline, net cost, quality countermeasure, and decision that followed.

Anticipate the gaps in your experience. Name the capability you have demonstrated, the capability you would build with a peer executive, and the early evidence you would seek in a new role. Avoid presenting a polished capstone as a substitute for experience you have not had.

example.title: A usable evidence index
example.body: Fictional capstone claim: 'I can design a disciplined AI investment process.' Evidence: board deck page 2 states the staged envelope; finance page 1 shows 15%, 30%, and 70% adoption cases; governance page 1 identifies claims VP release authority; decision log entry 3 records a held gate. Status: design capability shown by a hypothetical case, with no delivered business result. Separate real-work claim: 'I changed funding after evidence'; cite a truthful project story, your actual decision authority, and a verifiable result. If that story does not exist, remove the claim.

exercise.title: Make an evidence index
exercise.body: Choose five claims you would make in an interview. For each, link a real story and, where useful, a capstone artifact. Identify any claim supported only by a hypothetical exercise and rewrite it to describe capability rather than delivered results.

sources: NIST AI RMF Core: governance and measurement
OECD due diligence guidance for responsible AI

parts.label: Apply
parts.title: Run a rigorous portfolio interview
parts.body:
Give a reviewer the two-page memo and ask for a 30-minute discussion. Spend five minutes on the organization and requested decision, ten on economics and architecture, ten on risk and authority, and five on what changed after critique. Keep the full board deck available for evidence rather than presenting every slide by default.

Ask the reviewer to test three things: whether your claims distinguish observed from assumed results; whether you can defend the plan when a pivotal assumption fails; and whether you can describe your own role without taking credit for another function's authority. Record questions that required you to hunt through the material. Revise the evidence index or artifact so the answer is easy to find.

Finish with a one-page learning record: strongest evidence, biggest unresolved gap, a concrete development step, and the executive role or company context where your strengths fit. The purpose is to make career decisions with the same discipline used in the capstone.

example.title: A scored mock review
example.body: Fictional candidate's first mock review, four criteria scored 0–5 by a peer: clarity 4, evidence accuracy 2, decision judgment 3, and honesty about personal role 4, total 13/20. The reviewer found a CAD 400,000 'saved' label that actually described modeled capacity, and could not locate the stop gate. Candidate relabels realized savings as zero, adds volume and correction-cost assumptions, moves the gate to the decision cover, and repeats the review. Second scores: 4, 5, 4, and 5, total 18/20. A score is useful only with recorded observations and revisions; these scores are invented for instruction.

exercise.title: Complete the package
exercise.body: Submit the memo, board deck, architecture page, governance map, scorecard, and six stories. Have a reviewer score clarity, evidence, decision judgment, and honesty. Revise two artifacts based on the review and log the changes.

sources: UC Berkeley Career Engagement: interview preparation
